soil-chem-134.title: Pyrite, the fool's gold that turns to acid
soil-chem-134.text: Fool's gold has a sour side. Pyrite is iron sulfide, FeS2, the most common sulfide mineral. It occurs in igneous, metamorphic and sedimentary rocks. It is common in coal beds and in shale, where it precipitates from seawater that lacks oxygen. Exposed to oxygen and water, it breaks down into iron oxyhydroxides and sulfuric acid, a {{ref:soil-chem-113}} reaction that Acidithiobacillus bacteria speed up. Fine framboidal pyrite, made by sulfate-reducing bacteria in clayey muds, oxidizes faster still. That oxidation causes {{ref:soil-bio-059}}. In coal mines, spreading limestone dust neutralizes the acid and slows the reaction.
